evidence_item: Regional S3 object index/location metadata and placement capacity

boundaries.citation: 9:37AM PST command run under an established playbook
boundaries.note: Metadata intact before the removal command

boundaries.citation: one input entered incorrectly; a larger set of servers was removed than intended
boundaries.note: Capacity invariant (subsystem capacity >= minimum required) violated before any subsystem loses service

boundaries.citation: while these subsystems were being restarted, S3 was unable to service requests
boundaries.note: Index metadata unavailable downstream; recovery at 12:26PM (partial) and 1:18PM (full)

boundaries.citation: the placement subsystem began recovery when the index subsystem was functional and finished recovery at 1:54PM PST
boundaries.note: Shared-capacity nonlocal effect: placement depends on index and lost its own capacity in the same removal

candidates: incorrect command input removing a larger server set than intended
removal tool lacking a capacity-floor safeguard and slow-removal limit

postmortem_reference: AWS attributes the event to a command run with an incorrect input and states the tool allowed too much capacity to be removed too quickly; safeguards and cell partitioning were added.
notes: IL (capacity floor) precedes FL (index metadata unavailability). Shared capacity across billing/index/placement subsystems is the nonlocal channel.

evidence_item: East-coast database writes and their replication stream; secondarily, queued webhook events

boundaries.citation: loss of connectivity between our US East Coast network hub and our primary US East Coast data center; connectivity was restored in 43 seconds
boundaries.note: Replication stream unavailable during the partition; East writes briefly failed to reach West

boundaries.citation: the US West Coast data center and US East Coast public cloud Orchestrator nodes were able to establish a quorum and start failing over clusters
boundaries.note: Failover evidence (Raft quorum) remained available and was acted on

boundaries.citation: the database servers in the US East Coast data center contained a brief period of writes that had not been replicated to the US West Coast facility
boundaries.note: Divergence invariant violated: both sites held writes absent from the other; fail-back unsafe

boundaries.citation: we processed ~200,000 webhook payloads that had outlived an internal TTL and were dropped
boundaries.note: Second evidence item: queued events expired before delivery; TTL invariant violated at consumption time

candidates: Orchestrator promoting primaries across regional boundaries (behaved as configured)
network maintenance partition between hub and primary data center

postmortem_reference: GitHub states Orchestrator behaved as configured and the 43-second partition triggered the chain; it plans to prevent cross-region primary promotion.
notes: Two evidence items: replication stream (exception: upstream maintenance is a shared-state cause) and webhook queue (TTL expiry = acquisition loss at delivery; backlog replay is reacquisition for the surviving payloads).

evidence_item: Per-request evaluation capacity at the edge (continuous resource; applicability-boundary case)

boundaries.citation: these WAF rules were deployed globally in one go
boundaries.note: Deployment invariant (progressive rollout) violated although the rule itself ran in simulated mode and blocked no traffic

boundaries.citation: one of these rules contained a regular expression that caused CPU to spike to 100% on our machines worldwide
boundaries.note: Evaluation capacity unavailable downstream from 1342 UTC; global termination at 1409 UTC restored it

boundaries.citation: at its worst traffic dropped by 82%

candidates: catastrophic regex in the new managed rule
bypassing progressive deployment for the ruleset

postmortem_reference: Cloudflare attributes the outage to a single misconfigured WAF rule and states testing and deployment processes were insufficient; a global termination restored service.
notes: Boundary-of-applicability case: evidence here is a continuous resource (CPU capacity), not a discrete item; FLM still separates the violated rollout invariant from the capacity loss, but the evidence model maps weakly and the case is retained for that honest reason. Simulated mode provided a seat guarantee without an end-to-end guarantee.

evidence_item: BGP route advertisements mapping service addresses to reachable locations; secondarily, DNS-backed internal tooling

boundaries.citation: our systems are designed to audit commands like these to prevent mistakes like this, but a bug in that audit tool prevented it from properly stopping the command
boundaries.note: Admission invariant violated: a command that should have been blocked or confirmed was not

boundaries.citation: a command was issued with the intention to assess the availability of global backbone capacity, which unintentionally took down all the connections in our backbone network
boundaries.note: Backbone state destroyed by the maintenance action

boundaries.citation: making these locations declare themselves unhealthy and withdraw those BGP advertisements... our DNS servers became unreachable even though they were still operational
boundaries.note: Address evidence withdrawn downstream per the health-check design; a nonlocal cascade of the backbone state

boundaries.citation: the total loss of DNS broke many of the internal tools we'd normally use to investigate and resolve outages
boundaries.note: Second loss surface: investigation tooling lost its own evidence channel

candidates: maintenance command disconnecting the global backbone
audit-tool bug that failed to stop the command

postmortem_reference: Meta names both the maintenance command and the audit-tool bug, and describes the BGP withdrawal as a designed fail-safe reacting to backbone loss.
notes: The DNS health-check design is itself a nonlocal channel: an upstream state change converts into downstream evidence withdrawal. Investigation tooling breaking (DNS-dependent) is a meta-level evidence loss during response.

evidence_item: Customer site records (tenant state); secondarily, site identifiers and admin contact metadata used for support outreach

boundaries.citation: the API used to perform the deletion accepted both site and app identifiers and assumed the input was correct... there was no warning signal to confirm the type of deletion
boundaries.note: Identifier-type invariant violated at the API boundary: site IDs accepted where app IDs were intended

boundaries.citation: the result was an immediate deletion of 883 sites... between 07:38 UTC and 08:01 UTC
boundaries.note: Site records destroyed; monitoring did not observe it because the deletion ran through a standard workflow (observation gap)

boundaries.citation: the same script that deleted customer sites also deleted key customer identifiers... as a result, customers were blocked from filing technical support tickets
boundaries.note: Second evidence item: contact metadata destroyed, so the response path lost its own addressing evidence

boundaries.citation: our databases are backed up... immutable backups that are designed to be resilient against data corruption events
boundaries.note: Reacquisition source: 30-day immutable backups; Restoration 2 re-uses the old site identifiers, preserving lineage identity and removing the identifier re-mapping steps

candidates: communication gap passing site IDs where app IDs were intended
deletion API lacking an identifier-type guard or confirmation signal

postmortem_reference: Atlassian names the communication gap and the API's missing warning as the two problems; recovery used immutable backups and met the one-hour RPO while missing the RTO.
notes: Detection was bounded: internal monitoring observed nothing anomalous (P=? on the monitoring boundary), so the incident surfaced through a customer ticket at 07:46 UTC. Restoration 2's reuse of old identifiers is direct evidence that preserving lineage identity dominates re-mapping cost.
